newsitem.title: PERU: Fujimori slams rebels for celebrating bloody past.
newsitem.headline: Fujimori slams rebels for celebrating bloody past.

text.p: President Alberto Fujimori returned to Peru on Tuesday with harsh words for the rebels holding 72 hostages at the Japanese ambassador's home, slamming them for celebrating "acts of blood."
The rebels fired six shots into the air earlier on Tuesday and shouted slogans in memory of comrades whose deaths led to the formation of their Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA).
"They are showing themselves for what they are. Today they tried to celebrate an act of blood," Fujimori told reporters on landing at Lima's international airport.

Fujimori, arriving home after an emergency summit in Canada with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, was met by Defence Minister Tomas Castillo and Prime Minister Alberto Pandolfi and a 21-cannon salute.
Japan's point man in the crisis, Terusuke Tarada, who will observe any talks between the government and rebels, also met Fujimori after his four-day trip to Toronto and Washington.
Fujimori tempered his anger at the rebels by vowing to continue to look for a peaceful solution to the seven-week-old crisis.
"We are going to manage (the crisis) with due prudence and firmness," he said.

Following the gunfire earlier on Tuesday, one of the 15 guerrillas in the fortified compound gave a five-minute speech referring to a textile factory labour dispute in which the leader of the hostage-takers participated 18 years ago.
"Today, February 4, 1997, we pay homage to the comrade workers" who died in the strike at the Cromotex factory near Lima in 1979, the unidentified rebel shouted.
"Comrades, take our blood and transform it into the torrent of revolutionary force," the rebel shouted at the end of his speech.
The rebels then placed three new signs in an upper window of the diplomatic mansion commemorating the Cromotex dispute.
One participant in the 1979 strike was Nestor Cerpa Cartolini, the highest-ranking MRTA leader not currently in jail and the leader of the guerrillas inside the compound.

Tuesday's posturing from both sides flew in the face of Fujimori's claims while abroad that the government and rebels had laid the groundwork for a resumption of direct talks aimed at finding a solution to the seven-week siege.

Fujimori first agreed on Saturday in Toronto with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto to push for talks. Then in Washington on Sunday he announced the rebels were prepared to roll back their main demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.
Such a concession would allow fresh dialogue. Negotiations have been deadlocked for over a month because Fujimori refuses to consider the demand.
But the rebels reiterated they were sticking to their demand, leaving the sides entrenched in the same uncompromising positions they have held since the storming of the diplomatic mansion on Dec. 17.

In the first weeks of the current crisis, the rebels freed most of the 500 VIPs they originally took hostage. They still hold two government ministers, police chiefs, congressmen, judges, about two dozen Japanese businessmen and diplomats, the Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors and Fujimori's younger brother.
